## Analysis

**STORY:** This machine's autostart footprint is dominated by ordinary vendor auto-update infrastructure — OneDrive, Adobe, Google, Lenovo, HP, Office, Zoom — all sitting in their expected Program Files locations with matching scheduled tasks, and the Winlogon Shell/Userinit values are exactly `explorer.exe` and `userinit.exe,` with no logon hijack. What stands apart are two auto-start services — `CodexSandboxService.OpenAI.Codex` (DisplayName "ChatGPT") and `CoworkVMService` (DisplayName "Claude") — whose service-name/display-name pairing is atypical for how vendors normally register services, and whose `PathName` values were truncated in this collection so the actual executable location can't be confirmed. Two HKCU Run entries (Canva, Figma) launch from AppData, which is a user-writable location by the flagging rule, though this is common for Electron-style consumer apps. The decisive gap is that the service PathName column was cut off for the entire service list, so the unquoted-path privilege-escalation check (T1543.003) could not actually be performed — this is an evidence gap, not a clean result.

**KNOWN-GOOD:** `SecurityHealthSystray.exe` (system32) — standard Windows Security Center tray component. `OneDrive.exe` under `Program Files\Microsoft OneDrive` with matching OneDrive scheduled tasks — normal Microsoft cloud-sync deployment. Adobe/Google/Lenovo/HP/Office services and tasks — service names match their vendors and paths are consistent with normal installers. `MicrosoftEdgeAutoLaunch_...` under `Program Files (x86)\Microsoft\Edge` — standard Edge fast-startup feature. The lookalike that should **not** be waved through without a second look: the **Logitech Download Assistant** HKLM Run entry, which invokes `rundll32.exe` against `C:\Windows\System32\LogiLDA.dll` — an interpreter-launch pattern (T1547.001) that is historically legitimate for Logitech but is exactly the technique attackers copy, so it needs signature/hash verification rather than automatic trust.

**HYPOTHESES:**
- *CodexSandboxService.OpenAI.Codex / CoworkVMService ("Claude")* — Benign: genuine local sandbox/VM helper services shipped by OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude desktop apps for code execution. Hostile: malware registered under trusted AI-brand names to gain an autostart SYSTEM service. Settling evidence: full un-truncated `BINARY_PATH_NAME` from `sc qc <name>` plus `Get-AuthenticodeSignature` on that binary.
- *Canva / Figma AppData Run entries* — Benign: normal per-user Electron-app auto-launch agents. Hostile: payload staged in AppData under a trusted-looking name. Settling evidence: Authenticode signature and hash comparison of `Canva.exe` / `figma_agent.exe` against vendor-published installers.
- *Logitech Download Assistant rundll32 entry* — Benign: shipped LogiLDA.dll bundled with the Realtek/Logitech driver package. Hostile: a renamed malicious DLL placed in System32. Settling evidence: hash-check `LogiLDA.dll` against Logitech's known-good hash.

**PLAN:** (1) Cheapest and most decisive: `sc qc CodexSandboxService.OpenAI.Codex` and `sc qc CoworkVMService` to get the un-truncated path, then check the Authenticode signer — this resolves the highest-exploitability unknown fast. (2) Re-pull the full `Win32_Service.PathName` for all services (this output truncated it) to complete the unquoted-path check per T1543.003. (3) If either AI-branded service binary is unsigned or in an unexpected path, isolate the host and treat as active compromise. (4) Verify Canva/Figma binary signatures — lower urgency. (5) No Winlogon/Run-key hijack found, so no containment needed there; routine cleanup only.
